docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
Video and GIF follow the HTML slideshow's timing, except that nobody can click: on_click animations play automatically, one after another, like after_previous (PowerPoint's own video export does the same). Each slide plays its transition over the previous slide's last frame, runs its animations (starting with the transition, as in HTML), then holds its settled state for the transition's advance_after if set, otherwise for hold. In narrated MP4/WebM/MOV output, the inferred or explicit narration duration (or the silent-slide default) extends the visual slide when it is longer than advance_after. A slide with no transition cross-fades in over 0.5s (slide 0 with none starts instantly); set a transition on slide 0 to animate in from the matte, which also makes looping GIFs wrap smoothly.

GIF is encoded by Pillow with per-frame durations, so no extra dependency is needed. MP4 (H.264), WebM (VP9), and MOV (ProRes 4444) require the ffmpeg binary on PATH (or pointed to by the QUICKTHUMB_FFMPEG environment variable).

Canvas MP4, WebM, and MOV output can carry a soundtrack: any audio file ffmpeg decodes (MP3, WAV, AAC, OGG, ...), encoded as AAC in MP4/MOV and Opus in WebM:

mp4 = canvas.to_mp4(soundtrack="music.mp3")                    # loops to fill the video
mp4 = canvas.to_mp4(soundtrack="jingle.wav", loop_audio=False) # plays once, then silence

The audio is always trimmed to the video length. For an AudioTrack, loop=True repeats a shorter track and loop=False plays it once before silence; loop_audio is an explicit override. Legacy string paths keep the previous looping default. GIF exports do not accept a soundtrack.

Format limits

Canonical layer translation, rotation and scaling use subpixel bicubic affine sampling while geometry is moving. Still images, held geometry and settled endpoints retain their existing pixels, including nonidentity final transforms. Image viewport zoom/pan keeps its separate image-renderer behavior.

By default, frames are composited onto the opaque matte color (default black). VP9 WebM and ProRes MOV support opt-in alpha as described above; GIF and MP4 remain opaque. Mixed-size slides are scaled to fit and centered on the first slide's size. H.264/VP9 4:2:0 output needs even dimensions, so odd-sized canvases lose their last pixel row/column in MP4/WebM output. GIF encoding streams quantized frames through Pillow, keeping only a bounded number of uncompressed frames instead of imposing a timeline frame-memory budget. The final compressed GIF is still buffered in memory, including for file exports; large canvases, documents and encoded files can still exhaust available memory. max_size and colors remain useful for reducing output size. GIF dimensions and each coalesced frame duration must still fit the format’s 16-bit fields (65,535 pixels and 655.35 seconds). Animated Deck MP4/WebM/MOV accepts at most 64 slides with narration because each narration is decoded as a concurrent FFmpeg input; split larger narrated decks into multiple exports. Silent slides do not count toward this limit.

docs.title: Canonical samples
docs.text:
sample() returns the renderer-independent reference that exports are compared against, as a JSON-serializable FrameSequence. Canvas and Deck share the same contract, and a canvas produces the same observations as a one-slide deck containing it.

still = canvas.sample()                         # settled frame(s), as PNG/PDF/PPTX draw them
timed = deck.sample(fps=10)                     # uniform grid over the whole animated timeline
probe = deck.sample([0.0, 1.25, 4.0], hold=2.0) # explicit instants, ascending
  • Frames. Each CanonicalFrame holds width * height pixels as raw 8-bit RGBA (row-major from the top-left, sRGB, straight alpha), base64-encoded in data, plus the sha256 of those bytes. index is the frame's position in the sequence and slide the page it shows. A frame whose digest or dimensions do not match its data is rejected when it is loaded.
  • Still captures (capture="still") hold one frame per page in slide order, at each page's own size, with transparency preserved. time is None, duration is 0, and timeline is empty.
  • Timeline captures (capture="timeline") observe the timeline that animated WebM/MP4 exports play: transitions, Morph, layer animations, narration-driven slide durations, and a settled hold of hold seconds (default 3) for pages without an explicit duration. Frames are ordered by ascending time in seconds, share the first slide's size, and are composited onto the opaque matte (default black), which is reported as #RRGGBB. Deck GIF export currently ignores explicit and narration slide durations, so it matches this timeline only for decks without them.
  • Sampling. fps=N (at most 120) observes every instant k / N before duration; explicit times must be ascending, and times at or past duration show the final settled frame. One capture observes at most 100,000 instants; a larger explicit list or fps grid is rejected with a ValidationError before any frame renders. This grid is an observation schedule, not an exporter's frame schedule: exporters sample each span on their own frame grid, and stretch a slide shorter than one frame to a full frame.
  • Timing. duration is the exact timeline length and never depends on fps or on the requested instants. Each TimelineSegment gives a slide's absolute start, transition_end, animation_end, and end, rounded to nanoseconds; a slide is on screen over [start, end), so a boundary instant belongs to the incoming slide.
  • Memory. A capture whose distinct frames would exceed 768 MiB of raw RGBA is rejected with a ValidationError, before any frame renders when every page of a still capture, or one frame of a timeline capture, already exceeds it; request fewer instants, a lower fps, a shorter hold, or a smaller document.
  • Environment. sample() and export() report quickthumb, Pillow and FreeType versions, the text layout engine (basic or raqm), available RAQM/HarfBuzz/FriBidi versions, and the FFmpeg version for documents with video layers. Sampling video without a working FFmpeg raises RenderingError before any frame renders. environment.fonts reports the actual font face bytes selected by that operation; the asset manifest separately describes authored references.

docs.title: Render reproducibility
docs.text:
Font family names and QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT depend on the machine's font search path. Inspect the selected faces rather than treating those names as portable identifiers:

capture = canvas.sample()
for font in capture.environment.fonts:
    print(font.source, font.sha256, font.variations)

Each face has its resolved file path (or pillow:default), SHA-256 and applied variable coordinates keyed by the font's axis names. The hash identifies the font bytes. Pillow's embedded face reports no hash if its bytes are unavailable. Paths are diagnostic: compare hashes and coordinates across machines. Only faces loaded for the current operation are reported; unused named fonts and faces from earlier operations are excluded.

Remote and Google fonts load from content-addressed copies of their resolved bytes, so another document refreshing the original URL does not change a prefetched face. These copies live in the asset cache and follow its caller-owned cleanup lifecycle. Keep local input files unchanged during an operation.

For repeatable canonical raster output, use identical document data, input asset bytes, selected fonts and variable coordinates, rendering options and environment; seed procedural effects where supported. Different font, shaping or rasterizer versions can change layout and edge pixels. This report explains those inputs; it does not promise exact pixels across platforms or native-output viewers. Use format-specific fidelity tolerances when comparing such outputs.

docs.title: Remote assets and caching
docs.text:
render() and export() download remote images, SVGs, text fills, and fonts into a shared cache, and export() returns an asset_manifest describing every asset it used. prefetch_assets() is optional: it does the same downloads up front and returns the manifest without rendering, so you can catch network failures or stale entries before a long export, or warm the cache for offline renders. Each AssetManifestEntry has the source as written, its semantic asset_type, a status, and whatever identity it has: source_key (canonical URL), cache_key and cache_path, content_hash (SHA-256 of the bytes used), and fetched_at (UTC time of the download).

status Meaning local An existing local file. missing A local path that does not exist. network Downloaded now and written to the cache. fresh Read from a cache entry within max_age (always, when no max_age is set). stale Read from an expired cache entry, or while offline, because it could not be refreshed. stale_reason explains why. unresolved A remote reference that has not been resolved yet.

The cache is controlled by environment variables:

  • QUICKTHUMB_ASSET_CACHE_DIR: cache directory (default: the system temp directory).
  • QUICKTHUMB_ASSET_MAX_AGE: seconds after which a cached entry is refreshed from the network. When the refresh fails, the old bytes are used and reported as stale. Unset means cached entries never expire.
  • QUICKTHUMB_ASSET_OFFLINE=1: never make network requests. Cached entries are used, and expired ones are reported as stale.

docs.title: Ownership and reuse
docs.text:
Keep the same Canvas or Deck to reuse resolution across prefetch_assets(), sample(), and exports. Each canvas retains its first remote resolution result and status; a deck uses its slides' results. Remote images, text fills, and SVGs render from these retained bytes. Remote fonts, including Google fonts, load from content-addressed copies of the resolved bytes, so another document's URL refresh does not change a prefetched face. Keep those cache files available through sampling and export. Construct a new document to resolve the same reference again under the current cache policy.

PrefetchResult and asset_manifest are JSON-safe reports, not resource handles. Saving or loading their JSON does not transfer bytes or preload another document. A new document can reuse the persisted cache and reports fresh when its entry is usable. Local image, font, video, and audio paths remain caller-owned files: keep them available and unchanged through sampling or export; prefetch does not freeze or copy them. Video and audio sources are not downloaded by prefetch; remote video is read by FFmpeg when needed and is outside this cache contract. Generated content without a file/URL reference has no external asset entry.

The caller owns the cache directory and its cleanup. Quickthumb atomically writes remote cache files and metadata but does not automatically evict them. Remove unused entries only when documents and export workers are no longer using that cache; existing manifests are observations, not guarantees that their cache_path still exists. No explicit document close is required for the in-memory remote results: they are released with the document.

When neither a usable cache entry nor a network response exists, resolution raises RenderingError naming the source, the cause, and the cache directory it searched. To refuse stale inputs, check the manifest before rendering:

prefetched = canvas.prefetch_assets()
stale = [entry for entry in prefetched.asset_manifest if entry.status == "stale"]
if stale:
    raise SystemExit(f"stale assets: {[(e.source, e.stale_reason) for e in stale]}")

docs.title: Asset and plugin lifecycle fixtures
docs.text:
The shared font/texture scenarios in tests/test_asset_cache.py use a private plugin registry, a repository TTF and generated image bytes served by a temporary localhost HTTP server. They exercise public Canvas/Deck operations and cache environment settings. A controlled standard clock advances expiry without sleeping or editing cache files or metadata. No public network service or platform-specific pixel snapshot is required.

Scenario Observable evidence Regression check Network → fresh new document → expired refresh Resolution status, fetched time, changed content hashes, actual font identity and decoded PNG pixels; original documents retain their resolved bytes test_combined_resources_refresh_only_for_new_expired_documents (canvas, deck) Expired cache while offline Both resources report stale with source, hash, fetch time and offline/max-age reason before plugin execution or output; a caller proceeding gets the original RGBA/font bytes without requests test_combined_offline_stale_evidence_precedes_optional_rendering (canvas, deck) Cold offline font or plugin texture Public prefetch identifies the later slide, source URL and cache directory; plugin texture errors also identify the layer/asset path. No callback or file write occurs test_combined_cold_offline_failure_identifies_later_slide_resource (font, texture) Prefetched resources across raster and native document output Canvas/Deck raster agreement, actual font SHA, asset manifest, native SVG text and exact plugin PNG fallback test_prefetched_font_and_private_plugin_keep_shared_export_evidence Missing declared plugin dependency Escaped JSON Pointer, layer identity and prewrite failure test_plugin_declared_missing_assets_fail_before_output_or_callback Plugin native match, tolerated difference, mismatch or unsupported target Actual local SVG comparison and adopted native/PNG representation; explained fallback and strict rejection tests/test_plugin_svg.py, test_plugin_document_fallback_reports_and_preserves_output in tests/test_plugin_runtime.py Default, family, file and variable fonts Actual selected face hashes and applied coordinates in sample/export environments Font identity cases in tests/test_canonical_sampling.py

Stale refusal is a caller decision using the returned manifest, as shown above; there is no automatic refuse-stale export flag. The offline fixture verifies that evidence is available before any plugin callback or destination change, then separately verifies the caller's choice to render with those stale bytes. Cold misses fail rather than substituting a font or empty plugin texture.

Run uv run --locked pytest tests/test_asset_cache.py tests/test_plugin_runtime.py tests/test_plugin_svg.py tests/test_canonical_sampling.py --no-cov -q. These files are included in the existing automated pytest tests/ quality job. Named scenarios and parameter IDs identify the resource/document failure; expected hashes are computed from the controlled source bytes and rendered samples are compared in the same recorded font/render environment. This does not promise identical font pixels across machines or native viewers.

docs.title: Decks (multiple images and slides)
docs.text:
A Deck is an ordered list of canvases. Each slide is a full Canvas and renders exactly as it would on its own. See the Deck API reference for the full method list.

Give the deck a size once and each slide can be a bare Canvas() that inherits it:

from quickthumb import AudioTrack, Canvas, Deck, VideoOptions

deck = (
    Deck(1280, 720)   # default slide size; Deck.from_aspect_ratio("16:9", 1280) also works
    .slide(Canvas().background(color="#101820").text(content="Cover", size=96, color="#FFFFFF"))
    .slide(Canvas().background(color="#1A1A2E").text(content="Body", size=64, color="#FFFFFF"))
)
# pre-built canvases work too: Deck(slides=[cover, body])

deck.render("deck.pdf")     # one multi-page PDF (a page per slide)
deck.render("deck.pptx")    # one multi-slide PPTX (a slide per slide)
deck.render("deck.gif")     # one animation playing transitions between slides
deck.export("deck.mp4")     # animated slides with per-slide narration
deck.render(
    "deck.mp4",
    animation=VideoOptions(soundtrack=AudioTrack(path="music.mp3", loop=True)),
)  # animated + mixed audio
deck.render("animated.mp4", animation=VideoOptions(fps=20))  # animated, silent
deck.render("slides.png")   # numbered sequence: slides_01.png, slides_02.png, …

pdf_bytes = deck.to_pdf()
pptx_bytes = deck.to_pptx()
gif_bytes = deck.to_gif()
webm_bytes = deck.to_webm()
mp4_bytes = deck.to_mp4()   # timeline with per-slide narration

render() dispatches on the output extension: .pdf and .pptx produce a single document; .gif, .mp4, .webm, and .mov produce an animation; and raster extensions have no native multi-page container, so the deck writes one file per slide as a zero-padded numbered sequence and returns the written paths.

Slides may have different dimensions. deck.diagnose() aggregates each slide's diagnostics (each tagged with its slide_index) and adds a mixed-slide-size warning when they differ. The PDF path sizes each page to its slide, but PPTX has a single presentation size taken from the first slide, so slides larger than the first are clipped by PowerPoint. Keep slides the same size when targeting .pptx. Decks round-trip through JSON with deck.to_json() / Deck.from_json(...), reusing the per-canvas serialization.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The CLI picks the format from the output extension too:

quickthumb render spec.json -o card.svg
quickthumb render spec.json -o card.pptx
quickthumb render spec.json -o card.pdf

# Live HTML slides; open /?presenter for the presenter dashboard
quickthumb serve slides.py

docs.title: Lottie vectors
docs.text:
from quickthumb import Canvas, LottieOptions

canvas = Canvas(240, 160).shape("ellipse", (20, 20), 80, 60, "#159A8C")
result = canvas.export("scene.lot", animation=LottieOptions(fps=30, hold=3))

.lot contains ordinary Lottie JSON, not Quickthumb document JSON. The supported subset is a single Canvas: one initial solid background, solid rectangle/rounded rectangle, ellipse, pill, triangle, star and polygon shapes, and Paths (M/L/H/V/C/S/Q/T/A/Z) with even-odd solid fill or solid stroke. Shape alignment and percentage positions retain their authored layout. Path control hulls must fit inside the viewport (strokes reserve a conservative miter-limit margin); stroked Paths require uniform view-box scaling.

hold is nonnegative seconds; fps defaults to 30 and supports up to 120. Stroked degenerate contours are rejected rather than replaced with missing dots. The playback span is the latest canonical motion end plus hold, rounded up to whole frames; the receipt reports that frame count and its duration divided by fps. Zero hold adds no final pause; a static zero-hold composition still occupies one frame. Output has no audio or assets. See the runnable static example.

canvas.validate_export("lottie") lists unsupported source IDs and JSON paths. Gradients, effects/presets, stagger, masks, viewport clipping, paint/dash tracks, motion paths, images, plugins and Deck output are not supported in this slice. Export rejects them before opening the destination, including when a policy asks for static or raster fallback. It never silently drops features or embeds rendered frames. No Lottie import, ZIP or editor API is provided.

Quadratics convert exactly to cubic tangent handles. Elliptical arcs use the same bounded cubic conversion as native PDF paths (at most 1/8 device pixel approximation, with command and coordinate precision limits). No ReportLab or other document-renderer dependency is needed for Lottie. Closed contours retain their closing tangents and multiple contours share the even-odd fill rule. Admission uses the conservative control hull: some curves that visually fit are rejected when their controls exceed the fixed viewport. Rescale or reposition the path data inside its view box instead of expecting implicit cropping. See the curved Path example.

Canonical position, uniform/axis scale, rotation and opacity timelines retain ordered composition, easing, delays and held keys. Authored rotation is retained; track opacity multiplies authored layer opacity. Paths use their fixed viewport pivot. Shapes use the same whole painted-source pivot as canonical sampling, including authored static rotation, alignment and irregular geometry. Preparing an animated Shape uses one bounded untimed source probe to determine that pivot; it does not embed pixels. Animated Shape sources must fit inside the Canvas. Nonpositive uniform Shape/Null scale is explicitly unsupported by this renderer; axis scales and Path scales retain their canonical behavior.

Pose properties are held vector samples at LottieOptions.fps, augmented with exact event and authored-key boundaries shared across the Canvas. Between those instants the previous pose remains visible; output does not claim continuous native Lottie easing. Static properties remain native constants. Capability diagnostics report this sampling distinction. Export stops before writing if more than 100,000 total layer-pose observations or native coordinate precision limits would be exceeded. ExportPolicy(reduced_motion=True) intentionally removes the timelines and exports the authored static pose for hold seconds, rather than the animation endpoint. Other unsupported features still fail before writing. See the pose-motion example.

Top-level Null and supported Shape layers can form transform hierarchies with parent. Parenting composes existing canonical local frames, including authored rotation, anchors and nonuniform axes; local poses do not bake ancestors again. Percent coordinates still resolve against Canvas dimensions, even on children. Opacity affects each painted source independently and does not propagate from an invisible parent to its children. Axis-zero collapse and axis reflections retain the canonical parent behavior. Source drawing order remains independent of the graph order, including a child listed before its parent.

Linked Shape pivots retain the canonical opaque-reference footprint, even when the parent's own paint is transparent. Their local sources may begin outside the Canvas: ancestor transforms can bring them into view. Unlinked animated Shape sources keep the earlier unclipped-source requirement. Cycles, missing parents, unsupported groups/effects and Path parenting are rejected before writing. See the parenting example.

docs.title: Lottie stroke trim
docs.text:
Paths support authored trim_start, trim_end, trim_offset and their TrimStartTrack, TrimEndTrack, TrimOffsetTrack timelines. Trim uses one normalized local arc-length clock across all contours, including cyclic wrapped windows and negative or multi-turn offsets. Full 0→1 ignores offset; equal endpoints and 1→0 are empty. Fill remains complete underneath the trimmed stroke. Closed seams retain their joins; open cuts use the authored cap.

Trim properties use the same held fps samples, authored boundaries, composition, easing and reduced-motion policy as pose properties above. They remain native vector trim modifiers, with no frame images. Native endpoint rounding must not collapse a nonempty interval or exceed a conservative 1/8-pixel endpoint bound under the sampled scale; otherwise export rejects it before writing. The existing viewport, uniform stroke scaling and nondegenerate contour limits still apply. Dashes and dash-offset tracks remain unsupported; there is no trim-then-dash approximation. See the stroke-trim example.

docs.title: Lottie outlined text
docs.text:
Static plain single-line printable ASCII text exports as self-contained native cubic glyph outlines. Install quickthumb[lottie] for the optional fonttools dependency; shape and Path output do not require it. The actual resolved local FreeType face, including Pillow's embedded default font, supplies the outlines. The file embeds neither font assets nor editable Lottie text. Canonical baseline, alignment and explicit letter spacing determine glyph positions; font contour winding preserves holes within each independently painted glyph, so overlapping glyphs cannot cancel each other. Opacity applies once to the whole text layer. Text paint itself must be opaque: the canonical direct-draw alpha-paint behavior on a backdrop is not equivalent to native Lottie compositing.

Text must not use animation, parenting, rotation, wrapping/fitting, rich content, counters, effects, masks, gradients, variable/color fonts or remote font sources. Missing glyphs fail explicitly instead of becoming replacement boxes. Unspaced multi-character RAQM layout requires shaping and is rejected; use explicit nonzero letter_spacing. Unspaced BASIC text is admitted only when its measured advances are additive. This subset does not promise complex-script shaping.

Each layer is bounded to 1024 characters, 65536 outline vertices and a 64 MiB font source, with native coordinate-precision checks. Unsupported text and missing fonttools produce source-specific diagnostics before opening the destination. See the outlined-text example.

docs.title: Which Python versions are supported?
docs.text: Python 3.11 or later. The package is classified for 3.11 and 3.12, and CI runs on 3.11. This includes background removal (the rembg extra).

docs.title: The quickthumb command isn't found
docs.text: The command line tool is an optional extra: pip install "quickthumb[cli]". Installation lists every extra.

docs.title: Why does my SVG layer raise RenderingError?
docs.text: Drawing SVG files needs the svg extra: pip install "quickthumb[svg]". Exporting a canvas to SVG doesn't.

docs.title: What happens if I render a canvas with no layers?
docs.text: You get a fully transparent image of the canvas size. It isn't an error.

docs.title: Why does a group child raise "group children must not set position"?
docs.text:
A group positions its children itself. Remove position from the child and place the group instead:

canvas.group(
    children=[{"type": "text", "content": "TITLE", "size": 96, "color": "#FFFFFF"}],
    position=("8%", "50%"),
    align=("left", "middle"),
)

A child's align is ignored too. Use the group's item_align to line children up across the group.

docs.title: How do I check a design for problems before rendering?
docs.text: Call canvas.diagnose(), or run quickthumb lint spec.json on a JSON spec. It reports text that is too small or off the canvas, low contrast, hidden layers, and more. See Diagnostics & CLI.

docs.title: My text runs off the canvas
docs.text:
Set max_width so it wraps:

canvas.text(content="A longer title that needs two lines", size=72, color="#FFFFFF", max_width="60%")

Add auto_scale=True (with max_width, max_height, or both) to shrink the text until it fits instead.

docs.title: I set bold=True and weight=900 and got an error
docs.text: They set the same thing, so use one. weight is more precise: TextPart(text="STRONG", weight=900).

docs.title: How do I use a Google Font?
docs.text:
Name it and set font_source="google". It is downloaded once and cached, and weight picks the matching file:

canvas.text(content="Hello", font="Inter", font_source="google", weight=800, size=72, color="#FFFFFF")

You can also pass the URL of a font file, or point QUICKTHUMB_FONT_DIR at a folder of fonts. See Webfonts & Background Removal.

docs.title: Can I use images from a URL?
docs.text: Yes. background(image=...) and image(path=...) accept http(s) URLs. They are downloaded and cached while rendering. To control the cache, see Remote assets and caching.

docs.title: How do I remove the background behind a person?
docs.text:
Set remove_background=True on the image layer. It needs the rembg extra:

canvas.image(path="portrait.jpg", position=("75%", "55%"), width=420, height=520, remove_background=True)

docs.title: What's the difference between cover, contain, and fill?
docs.text: cover fills the box and crops what doesn't fit. contain fits the whole image inside the box and leaves empty space. fill stretches the image to the box, ignoring its proportions.

docs.title: Which formats can I export?
docs.text:
The format comes from the file extension you pass to render():

Kind Formats Needs Images PNG, JPEG, WebP Vector and documents SVG, PDF, PPTX pdf / pptx extras for PDF and PPTX Web HTML Animation GIF, MP4, WebM ffmpeg for MP4 and WebM

See Exporting for what each format keeps and loses.

docs.title: Can I set quality for a PNG?
docs.text: No. quality only applies to JPEG and WebP; passing it for PNG raises RenderingError.

docs.title: How do I get the image without writing a file?
docs.text:
png_base64 = canvas.to_base64(format="PNG")
jpeg_data_url = canvas.to_data_url(format="JPEG", quality=90)

docs.title: Can I pass a dict to Canvas.from_json()?
docs.text: No, it takes a JSON string. Convert first with json.dumps(data).

docs.title: Why does to_json() raise ValidationError?
docs.text: The canvas has a .custom(fn) layer. A Python function can't be written to JSON, so remove that layer first.

docs.title: My theme block disappeared after to_json()
docs.text: Theme tokens are replaced with their values when the spec is loaded, so to_json() writes the values and no theme block. Keep your original spec file if you want to keep editing the tokens.

docs.title: What do the different errors mean?
docs.text:
• ValidationError: an argument or spec field is invalid. Raised as soon as you add the layer or load the spec.
  • RenderingError: something failed while drawing, such as a download.
  • MissingAssetError: a local file the spec refers to doesn't exist.

Every error has details with a stable code, the JSON Pointer of the field, and the layer id. See Structured Errors.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide walks through the core workflow: create a canvas, add layers, and export an image.

docs.title: First export without fonts or downloads
docs.text:
First install quickthumb 0.8.0 in an isolated environment. In the working directory outside the checkout, save this as first_export.py. It needs only the base package and local disk:

from pathlib import Path

from quickthumb import Canvas

canvas = Canvas(320, 180).background(color="#102030").shape(
    "rectangle", position=(24, 24), width=96, height=64, color="#42CEB7",
)
Path("scene.json").write_text(canvas.to_json(), encoding="utf-8")
result = canvas.export("first.png")
print(result.written_paths)
print(result.pixel_metrics.width, result.pixel_metrics.height)

Run python first_export.py. It writes first.png (320 × 180) and the canonical scene description scene.json. result is an export receipt, separate from the editable scene JSON; the example prints its paths and dimensions. See the output API for diagnostics and other receipt fields.

With the cli extra installed, check requirements and render that same scene:

quickthumb doctor png --spec scene.json -o from-json.png
quickthumb render scene.json -o from-json.png

doctor checks discovered requirements and write permissions; the render command is the actual output check. Diagnostics & CLI explains its limits. JSON round trips explain what the scene file carries.

docs.title: Add typography to your thumbnail
docs.text:
This next example downloads Inter from Google Fonts on first use. It needs network access then, or a previously populated font cache. Use a local font path instead when working offline; the first export above needs no font setup.

from quickthumb import Canvas, LinearGradient, Shadow, Stroke, TextPart

canvas = (
    Canvas.from_aspect_ratio("16:9", base_width=1280)
    .background(
        gradient=LinearGradient(
            angle=135,
            stops=[("#0A1730", 0.0), ("#1F56C5", 1.0)],
        ),
    )
    .background(color="#000000", opacity=0.45)
    .text(
        content=[
            TextPart(
                text="BUILD THUMBNAILS\nFAST\n",
                color="#B8FF00",
                effects=[Stroke(width=8, color="#000000")],
            ),
            TextPart(
                text="With Python or JSON specs",
                color="#F5F5F5",
                size=44,
                effects=[Shadow(offset_x=2, offset_y=2, color="#000000", blur_radius=4)],
            ),
        ],
        font="Inter",
        font_source="google",
        size=112,
        position=("8%", "50%"),
        align=("left", "middle"),
        weight=900,
    )
    .outline(width=14, color="#B8FF00")
)

canvas.render("thumbnail.png")
thumbnail.png · 1280 × 720

docs.title: 1. Create a canvas
docs.text:
from quickthumb import Canvas

# Explicit size
canvas = Canvas(1280, 720)

# Or from an aspect ratio
canvas = Canvas.from_aspect_ratio("16:9", base_width=1280)
canvas = Canvas.from_aspect_ratio("1:1", base_width=1080)
canvas = Canvas.from_aspect_ratio("9:16", base_width=1080)

docs.title: 2. Add a background
docs.text:
from quickthumb import Canvas, Filter, LinearGradient

canvas = (
    Canvas(1280, 720)
    # Solid color
    .background(color="#0F172A")
    # Gradient overlay
    .background(
        gradient=LinearGradient(
            angle=120,
            stops=[("#111827", 0.0), ("#11182700", 1.0)],
        ),
        opacity=0.7,
    )
    # Remote image with effects
    .background(
        image="https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1516321318423-f06f85e504b3",
        fit="cover",
        blend_mode="multiply",
        effects=[Filter(blur=4, brightness=0.75)],
    )
)

Layers stack in call order: the first .background() is drawn first, at the back.

docs.title: 3. Add text
docs.text:
from quickthumb import Background, Glow, Shadow, Stroke, TextPart

canvas.text(
    content=[
        TextPart(text="5 ", color="#FBBF24", weight=900),
        TextPart(text="WARNING SIGNS", color="#FFFFFF", weight=900),
    ],
    size=72,
    position=(80, 540),
    effects=[
        Background(color="#111827CC", padding=(16, 22), border_radius=12),
        Stroke(width=2, color="#000000"),
        Shadow(offset_x=4, offset_y=4, color="#000000", blur_radius=8),
        Glow(color="#F59E0B", radius=14, opacity=0.35),
    ],
)

content can also be a plain string for simple cases:

canvas.text(content="Hello World", size=64, color="#FFFFFF", align="center")

docs.title: 4. Add an image
docs.text:
from quickthumb import Filter, Shadow

canvas.image(
    path="portrait.png",
    position=("73%", "52%"),
    width=420,
    height=520,
    fit="cover",
    align=("center", "middle"),
    border_radius=24,
    effects=[
        Filter(contrast=1.1, saturation=1.05),
        Shadow(offset_x=0, offset_y=12, color="#000000", blur_radius=24),
    ],
)

docs.title: 5. Add shapes
docs.text:
from quickthumb import Shadow, Stroke

canvas.shape(
    shape="rectangle",
    position=(64, 60),
    width=320,
    height=88,
    color="#CC0000",
    border_radius=10,
    effects=[
        Stroke(width=2, color="#FFFFFF"),
        Shadow(offset_x=0, offset_y=6, color="#000000", blur_radius=12),
    ],
)

docs.title: 6. Check your work
docs.text:
diagnose() flags common problems before you render, such as layers off the canvas, text too small to read, words that can't wrap, and low contrast:

for finding in canvas.diagnose().findings:
    print(finding.severity, finding.code, finding.message)

An empty findings list means the composition is clean. See Diagnostics & CLI.

docs.title: 7. Export
docs.text:
# PNG file
canvas.render("output.png")

# JPEG or WebP with quality
canvas.render("output.webp", format="WEBP", quality=90)
canvas.render("output.jpg", format="JPEG", quality=85)

# Base64 string
png_b64 = canvas.to_base64(format="PNG")

# Data URL (e.g. for HTML src=)
data_url = canvas.to_data_url(format="JPEG", quality=90)

docs.title: JSON workflow
docs.text:
You can also drive quickthumb from a JSON config instead of Python code:

from quickthumb import Canvas

config = """
{
  "kind": "canvas",
  "width": 1280,
  "height": 720,
  "layers": [
    { "type": "background", "color": "#111827" },
    {
      "type": "text",
      "content": "Hello quickthumb",
      "size": 72,
      "color": "#FFFFFF",
      "align": "center",
      "position": ["50%", "50%"]
    },
    { "type": "outline", "width": 10, "color": "#22C55E" }
  ]
}
"""

canvas = Canvas.from_json(config)
canvas.render("hello.png")

This is particularly useful for AI-generated specs. See JSON Schema & AI Workflow for details.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: quickthumb needs Python 3.11 or later.

docs.title: Isolated environment
docs.text:
The first-export guide uses the 0.8.0 API, including Canvas.export(). Install the release in a virtual environment outside any quickthumb checkout:

mkdir -p quickthumb-first-export
cd quickthumb-first-export
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install "quickthumb[cli]==0.8.0"

On Windows, activate with .venv\Scripts\activate instead. Omit [cli] when using only the Python API. The shell commands above use Bash/Zsh. Installing dependencies needs the package index or a populated local cache. Running outside the checkout ensures Python imports the installed wheel rather than the source directory.

docs.title: Existing uv project
docs.text: uv add "quickthumb[cli]>=0.8.0"

docs.title: Development checkout
docs.text:
To try unreleased changes, run uv build in the repository, then install the resulting wheel into the isolated environment using its absolute path, for example python -m pip install "/path/to/dist/quickthumb-0.8.0-py3-none-any.whl[cli]". This installs the checkout's code rather than downloading the published release. See the 0.8.0 migration notes when upgrading from 0.7.0.

The base package is enough for PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, SVG output, and HTML. Try the font-free first export before adding optional renderers.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
Some features need extra packages. Install them by name, for example pip install "quickthumb[svg,pdf]".

Extra Adds Needed for svg cairosvg canvas.svg(...) layers. Without it, rendering an SVG layer raises RenderingError. Exporting to SVG doesn't need it. pdf reportlab, fonttools, pypdfium2 PDF export and opt-in PDF fidelity observation pptx python-pptx .to_pptx() and render("out.pptx") lottie fonttools Self-contained supported text outlines in Canvas .lot exports; shape-only Lottie does not need this extra rembg rembg, onnxruntime remove_background=True on image layers. Requires Python 3.11+; downloads a model of about 170 MB on first use. cli typer, watchfiles, jinja2 The quickthumb command: render, lint, watch, serve, doctor, and more

MP4, WebM, and MOV export also need ffmpeg, which is a system program rather than a Python package:

brew install ffmpeg      # macOS
sudo apt install ffmpeg  # Debian / Ubuntu

MOV requires an FFmpeg build with the prores_ks encoder.

Rendering SVG layers uses CairoSVG and its native Cairo library; installing the Python extra does not install system libraries. The optional SVG fidelity observer also uses CairoSVG. See CairoSVG installation for platform requirements. The pdf extra includes PDFium bindings for PDF observation; plain PNG output needs neither renderer.

docs.title: Check your environment
docs.text:
quickthumb doctor (from the cli extra) discovers requirements for an export:

quickthumb doctor            # PNG, the default
quickthumb doctor mp4        # discover ffmpeg/ffprobe
quickthumb doctor pdf --spec card.json -o out/card.pdf

It exits with status 1 if a required check fails, so it also works as a CI step. It does not render a test file or certify native libraries, codec support, or visual fidelity. Run the intended export as well. See Diagnostics & CLI for details.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
All optional.

Variable What it does QUICKTHUMB_FONT_DIR Folder of font files to search when font is a family name QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT Font to use when a text layer has no font QUICKTHUMB_FONT_CACHE_DIR Where downloaded fonts are cached (default: the system temp folder) QUICKTHUMB_ASSET_CACHE_DIR Where downloaded images are cached (default: the system temp folder) QUICKTHUMB_ASSET_MAX_AGE Seconds before a cached download is refreshed. Unset means never. QUICKTHUMB_ASSET_OFFLINE Set to 1 to never download; only cached files are used QUICKTHUMB_FFMPEG, QUICKTHUMB_FFPROBE Paths to ffmpeg and ffprobe if they aren't on PATH

Remote assets and caching explains the cache in more detail.

docs.title: description: The quickthumb JSON spec format: document structure, the published JSON Schema, theme tokens, plugin layers, and every layer and effect.
JSON Schema & AI Workflow
docs.text: Any quickthumb canvas can be written as JSON. A JSON spec can be generated by an LLM or a template, stored in a database, sent through an API, or kept in version control next to your content.

docs.title: Round-trip serialization
docs.text:
Canonical JSON stores the authored document, separately from an export receipt:

from pathlib import Path

from quickthumb import Canvas

# Python → JSON
canvas = Canvas(320, 180).background(color="#102030")
json_str = canvas.to_json()
Path("scene.json").write_text(json_str, encoding="utf-8")

# JSON → Python
restored = Canvas.from_json(Path("scene.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
assert restored.to_json() == json_str
restored.export("from-json.png")

Note

Canvas.from_json() expects a JSON string. If you have a Python dict, call json.dumps(data) first. Canvases with .custom(fn) layers can't be serialized, because a Python function can't be stored as JSON.

Canonical serialization is deterministic for the same resolved document. It does not package fonts, images, media or cached downloads: retain referenced files and make their paths available when rendering elsewhere. Plugin JSON retains declared parameters and asset references, not Python callbacks; supply the matching explicit registry when loading it. Identical scene JSON does not guarantee identical pixels across fonts, renderer versions or platforms.

docs.title: JSON structure
docs.text:
A Canvas JSON document has four required top-level fields, plus an optional theme block:

{
  "kind": "canvas",
  "width": 1280,
  "height": 720,
  "theme": { ... },
  "layers": [ ... ]
}

The top-level "kind" discriminator is required (by Canvas.from_json(), Deck.from_json(), and the CLI) and must be "canvas" or "deck". Canvas documents carry layers; Deck documents carry slides and may also define a shared default size, theme, and transitions. Every layer object requires its own "type" discriminator field. Layers render in array order: the first item is at the back. Layer identity, placement, alignment and motion use the same shared vocabulary in Python, a Canvas JSON root and every Deck slide. A Deck does not introduce a different layer schema.

docs.title: Published schema
docs.text:
Emit the current JSON Schema from the same Pydantic models used by Canvas.from_json():

quickthumb schema > quickthumb.schema.json
quickthumb schema --output quickthumb.schema.json
quickthumb schema --document --output quickthumb.document-schema.json

The same schemas are available from Python as canvas_json_schema() and document_json_schema(), and hosted with these docs:

  • https://quickthumb.solaqua.dev/schema.json (Canvas)
  • https://quickthumb.solaqua.dev/document-schema.json (Canvas or Deck)

To get completion and validation while editing specs in VS Code, map your spec files to the hosted schema in .vscode/settings.json:

{
  "json.schemas": [
    {
      "fileMatch": ["*.thumb.json"],
      "url": "https://quickthumb.solaqua.dev/schema.json"
    }
  ]
}

Use a file mapping like this rather than a "$schema" key inside the spec: Canvas.from_json() rejects unknown top-level fields, including $schema.

The hosted files are regenerated on every docs deploy, which follows the main branch. Run quickthumb schema to get the schema for the version you have installed.

Schema scope

quickthumb schema describes concrete Canvas specs for external tooling and constrained generation. Use quickthumb schema --document for the combined Canvas/Deck discriminator schema. Canvas.from_json() remains the source of truth for what quickthumb can load.

The CLI, serve, Canvas.from_json(), and Deck.from_json() all require the matching top-level kind discriminator. Newly serialized documents include the discriminator at every document boundary, including Deck slides.

Deck slides may omit width and height when the Deck supplies default dimensions; the document schema accepts that form and canonical JSON emits the inherited dimensions on each slide. Transition objects use the same discriminated, strict contract as Deck.from_json().

Authoring conveniences such as $theme.* are resolved by quickthumb before model validation, so generic JSON Schema validators may reject unresolved authoring specs that quickthumb itself can load.

The command writes deterministic JSON only, so it can be checked into a repo, piped into an editor, or passed directly to a constrained-generation API. The Canvas schema includes the current canvas fields, built-in layer discriminators, effects, animations, supported platform presets, and the optional top-level theme block. The --document schema adds the Deck root and maps both document kinds through kind.

docs.title: Plugin layers
docs.text:
Plugin registrations are kept in one explicit PluginRegistry. A registration describes a layer type and its parameters. A separate trusted synchronous raster callback renders plugin layers as canonical RGBA pixels. Callbacks are application code, never serialized or imported from JSON.

from quickthumb import Canvas, PluginRegistry, canvas_json_schema

registry = PluginRegistry()
registry.register(
    "brand_badge",
    "1.0",
    params_schema={
        "type": "object",
        "required": ["label"],
        "properties": {"label": {"type": "string"}},
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
)

canvas = Canvas.from_json(text, registry=registry)
schema = canvas_json_schema(registry=registry)

A plugin layer requires type: "plugin", renderer, version, object-valued params, and positive integer width/height. position accepts the normal pixel/percentage coordinates; align and opacity affect its local box. Standard clip and mask boundaries apply after rendering. A Group controls child placement and can animate the whole group, including static plugin pixels. The same explicit registry must be supplied to document parsers and Schema helpers.

from PIL import Image

def badge(params, context):
    with Image.new("RGBA", context.size, params["color"]) as image:
        return image.tobytes()

registry.register("badge", "1", raster=badge)
canvas = Canvas(320, 180, registry=registry).plugin(
    "badge", version="1", params={"color": "#42CEB7"},
    position=(20, 30), width=120, height=40,
)
canvas.export("badge.png")

The callback receives a detached params dictionary and context.size. It must return exactly width * height * 4 raw RGBA8 bytes with straight alpha; it never receives the backdrop or an output file. Declare byte inputs as assets={"texture": "assets/texture.png"} on the layer and read them with context.read_asset("texture"). Only declared names are accepted. Reads use the shared asset resolver's cache, offline policy and remote download limits. Plugin code remains trusted Python: the helper is not a filesystem or process sandbox.

Canvas/Deck still and timed sampling, animation output and groups share the canonical renderer. By default SVG, HTML, PDF and PPTX embed plugin pixels as PNG fragments. Capability and export reports identify the renderer/version and fallback. ExportPolicy(unsupported_motion="error") rejects that fallback before writing; PPTX can also require native output per layer with pptx={"badge": "native"}. No time argument or animation callback is provided: the callback supplies static content, while group motion and slide transitions animate its composition. workers>1 rejects plugins because process-local callables are not serialized.

docs.title: Optional native SVG
docs.text:
Register svg= alongside the required raster= callback. Both receive detached params and the same PluginRenderContext; SVG returns a complete static SVG string. registry.capabilities("badge", "1") discovers registered implementations without executing callbacks. Replacing/unregistering a registration removes its old callbacks. Callbacks remain trusted Python and are never serialized.

from quickthumb import ExportPolicy

def badge_svg(params, context):
    width, height = context.size
    return (
        f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="{width}" height="{height}">'
        f'<rect width="{width}" height="{height}" fill="{params["color"]}"/></svg>'
    )

registry.register("badge", "1", replace=True, raster=badge, svg=badge_svg)
result = canvas.export("badge.svg", policy=ExportPolicy(fidelity={"svg": {
    "pixel_tolerance": 0, "max_different_pixel_ratio": 0, "min_hash_similarity": 1,
}}))

Explicit limits enable a Cairo comparison of the plugin's local RGBA region, including opacity. Only an exact/tolerated candidate becomes an isolated data:image/svg+xml image. Local measurements and reasons belong to executed plugin/representation diagnostics; pixel_metrics.fidelity separately measures the final whole SVG. This observes Cairo, not every SVG viewer. Validation alone reports an unmeasured candidate.

Absent limits/callbacks, rejected candidates and atomic clip/mask/parent composites retain canonical PNG pixels with a reason. Strict unsupported-motion policy fails before replacing output when a fallback is needed. The existing explicit fidelity policy requires Cairo even if the selected route is PNG. Only internal # references are accepted: external/data URI resources, imports, scripts, foreign HTML and SVG animation are rejected. Derive geometry/paint from declared read_asset() bytes instead. HTML/PDF/PPTX have no native plugin hook.

prefetch_assets() resolves every declared plugin asset without running the callback. Shared exports resolve them before writing, including declarations the callback does not read. Prefetch/export and observed inspection manifests report these references with asset_type="plugin", the original source, cache identity, SHA-256 and normal local/network/fresh/stale status. Repeated remote reads on the same document use its first resolved bytes; new documents follow the shared cache's refresh/offline policy. Local files remain caller-owned and must stay unchanged through export. Multiple declared names for one source share one manifest entry; the names remain in the layer's JSON.

Plugin assets are opaque bytes, not automatically validated images or selected font faces. Declaring a font file records its bytes, not any font selection or shaping a callback performs itself. The callback owns decoding and any resources it opens. Inspection reports observed state and may run the callback as part of normal diagnostics; it does not promise to prefetch unused references. Both Canvas and Deck inspection use the same plugin rendering and asset records.

docs.title: Plugin params Schema v1
docs.text:
params_schema accepts the documented quickthumb plugin-params v1 subset. It supports the JSON types object, array, string, number, integer, boolean, and null; required, properties, additionalProperties, items; const, enum, oneOf, anyOf; string patterns and size limits; and numeric minimum/maximum limits. Unsupported keywords such as $ref, allOf, and not are rejected during registration so the published Schema and runtime validation stay in agreement.

The process-global plugin_registry remains available for applications that want a shared default. For tests, services, and libraries, prefer an explicit PluginRegistry so registrations stay isolated and reproducible.

For constrained generation, prefer concrete resolved values in typed fields:

Use quickthumb.schema.json as the JSON response schema.
Generate one valid quickthumb canvas spec for a 1280x720 YouTube thumbnail.
Return only the JSON object.
Use concrete hex colors and numeric sizes in layer fields.
Use only these layer type discriminators: background, text, image, shape, svg, group, outline.

docs.title: Theme tokens
docs.text:
Define brand tokens once in a top-level theme block and reference them anywhere in the spec with $theme.path:

{
  "kind": "canvas",
  "width": 1280,
  "height": 720,
  "theme": {
    "colors": { "primary": "#B8FF00", "ink": "#111111" },
    "sizes": { "title": 96 }
  },
  "layers": [
    { "type": "background", "color": "$theme.colors.ink" },
    { "type": "text", "content": "Hello", "size": "$theme.sizes.title", "color": "$theme.colors.primary" }
  ]
}

Rules:

  • The theme block can nest groups arbitrarily; reference paths with dots: $theme.colors.primary.
  • A whole-string reference keeps its native JSON type: "size": "$theme.sizes.title" resolves to the number 96, and tokens can hold lists too.
  • Scalar tokens (strings, numbers) can also be embedded inside longer strings.
  • Theme values may reference other theme tokens (aliases). Circular references raise ValidationError.
  • Referencing an undefined token raises ValidationError.
  • Tokens are resolved at parse time: to_json() emits resolved values without the theme block.
  • Theme tokens work alongside $var template substitution (quickthumb render --var KEY=VALUE); $theme.* references are never treated as variables.

docs.text: The most common layers are shown below. Video, chart, QR code, counter, and plugin layers follow the same pattern; their fields are in the published schema and on their API reference pages.

docs.title: Group layer
docs.text:
Auto-layout container: children are measured and stacked along a row or column, so they must not set position. See the Group reference.

{
  "type": "group",
  "direction": "column",
  "gap": 24,
  "padding": 0,
  "position": ["8%", "50%"],
  "align": ["left", "middle"],
  "item_align": "start",
  "children": [
    { "type": "shape", "shape": "pill", "width": 120, "height": 36, "color": "#E94560" },
    { "type": "text", "content": "AUTO LAYOUT", "size": 96, "color": "#FFFFFF", "weight": 900 },
    { "type": "text", "content": "No coordinates were harmed", "size": 40, "color": "#A2A8D3" }
  ]
}
  • direction: "column" (default) or "row"
  • gap: pixels between children; padding: int, [vertical, horizontal], or [top, right, bottom, left]
  • item_align: cross-axis placement, one of "start", "center", or "end"
  • children types: "text", "image", "shape", "svg", or nested "group"

docs.title: Serialization notes
docs.text: Field Serialized form align String: "center", "top-left", etc. blend_mode String: "multiply", "normal", etc. fit String: "cover", "contain", "fill" position JSON array: [640, 360] or ["50%", "50%"] Gradient stops JSON array of ["#color", 0.0] pairs null fields Omitted fields default to null / their default value theme block Resolved at parse time; to_json() emits resolved values without the theme block

docs.title: Animation timing
docs.text: Use seconds for authored motion, slide durations, holds, video placement and caption cues. sample() observes the canonical timeline; export() reports the visual timeline actually encoded. Those measurements serve different purposes.

docs.title: Choose the clock
docs.text:
Output or observation Timing contract sample() with no time or fps One authored-static frame per Canvas/page, matching raster output without seeking an animation endpoint; duration=0, frame time=None. sample(time=...) Observe explicit document times. Slide windows are [start, end); an exact boundary belongs to the incoming slide. Times beyond the end show the settled final scene. sample(fps=...) Observe a uniform grid 0, 1/fps, 2/fps, … before the timeline end. A zero-length timeline is still observed once at zero. GIF Silent, variable frame durations in 10 ms steps; identical frames can coalesce. Default sampling rate 20 fps; supported rate is greater than zero and at most 100 fps. MP4 / WebM / MOV Constant-rate encoded frames, including repeated held frames. Default 30 fps; supported rate is greater than zero and at most 120 fps. HTML Browser-driven, interactive cues and slide navigation. No encoded fps or fixed total playback duration, and no Deck narration playback.

GifOptions.fps and VideoOptions.fps request the sampling density. Moving spans are sampled within their own timing boundaries; static spans become held shots. Video allocates repeated frames on a cumulative frame clock, while GIF quantizes cumulative durations to centiseconds. A canonical uniform sample grid is therefore not an index into the encoded file: arbitrary fractional spans, palette/lossy encoding and duplicate-frame coalescing can change frame positions or counts.

Read ExportResult.timing_metrics after an animated export:

Field Meaning fps The selected sampling rate; for GIF this is not stored frames divided by playback duration. frame_count Frames actually encoded, after GIF coalescing or video hold repetition. duration Encoded visual playback seconds: summed GIF delays or video frame count divided by fps. Audio container padding can differ.

FrameSequence.duration instead describes the unquantized canonical timeline. HTML returns no fixed playback timing in timing_metrics; its zero duration is not a claim that its interactive animations take no time.

from quickthumb import AnimationSpec, Canvas, GifOptions

canvas = Canvas(160, 90).background(color="#000000").shape(
    "rectangle", (40, 20), 80, 50, "#FF0000",
    animation=AnimationSpec.fade(duration=1),
)
samples = canvas.sample(fps=7, hold=0.37)
result = canvas.export("timed.gif", animation=GifOptions(fps=7, hold=0.37))
print(samples.duration, len(samples.frames))
print(result.timing_metrics.model_dump())

docs.title: Temporal exposure
docs.text:
Opt into centered motion blur when exporting a Canvas or Deck:

from quickthumb import MotionBlur, VideoOptions

canvas.export(
    "exposure.mp4",
    animation=VideoOptions(fps=30, motion_blur=MotionBlur(samples=8, shutter_angle=180)),
)

GifOptions and ImageSequenceOptions accept the same setting. None is the only off setting; MotionBlur accepts 2–64 samples and a positive shutter angle up to 360 degrees. The shutter spans (angle / 360) / fps seconds around each rendered frame. Instants outside the document timeline use its boundary state. Hard cuts bound the exposure to the slide on the center's side of the cut; an exact cut time belongs to the incoming slide. Smooth transitions participate in the exposure, including samples on either side of their start time. Video and image-sequence exposure centers follow the output grid index / fps; GIF centers follow its variable-duration shot clock. The encoded-sRGB premultiplied channels are averaged before returning straight RGBA, preserving saturated colors in transparent trails.

Exposure also integrates timed captions and appearances. They can contribute within half a shutter window of a cue boundary. Authored cue times and playback length remain unchanged; GIF delays and video frame counts still follow their codec clocks. With zero hold, the last frame is an exposure of motion. Add a hold to show an entirely settled frame.

This setting supports Canvas and Deck GIF/video exports and image sequences, including workers. Each worker computes a complete exposure with the same sample times and alpha accumulation as serial rendering. Direct byte helpers do not support this setting. sample() and render_frame() remain instantaneous canonical observations. Export receipts identify the requested temporal exposure in their capability report; source inspection cannot infer an export-only setting.

docs.title: Support and receipts
docs.text:
capabilities_for(target)["motion_blur"] declares temporal-exposure support:

Target family Support Meaning video full Canvas/Deck MP4, WebM, MOV and image sequences integrate the exposure. raster partial, static fallback Animated GIF integrates it; static raster files have no exposure window. html, pptx unsupported, static fallback Exposure is ignored; the authored browser/PowerPoint motion remains unchanged.

VideoOptions/GifOptions belong to their animated output families; passing them to HTML/PPTX raises an option-family error. The capability table does not make those options silently accepted. inspect_motion() reports source-authored features and does not claim that export-only blur was enabled. After an actual export, find the motion_blur row in result.capability_report for the applied sample count and angle; timing_metrics retains the encoded playback facts. Image-sequence results carry the same applied row and their frame/duration facts.

Run the moving-marker example to write matching OFF/8-sample GIFs. Its scene also drives the controlled sample-cost benchmark.

docs.title: Slide duration and transitions
docs.text:
Layer motion and the incoming transition start on the same slide clock. For noninteractive media, on_click cues run in sequence like after_previous; with_previous cues overlap. Delays are part of those clocks. Transitions play over the previous slide's settled scene; a slide without an explicit transition starts instantly on the first slide and uses a 0.5-second crossfade thereafter. Use Cut() for an immediate boundary.

A slide's exit is determined by the latest applicable boundary:

  • With neither a duration override nor advance_after, transition and layer motion finish, then the settled scene holds for hold seconds (default 3).
  • For Deck video, slide(duration=...) sets a total slide window, including its transition and motion. Without an explicit duration, narration supplies that window. Neither trims a longer visual animation; the slide lasts long enough for both. Narration itself is trimmed or padded to its scheduled window.
  • A transition's advance_after replaces hold: its boundary is counted after the incoming transition. The exit is the latest of that boundary, completed motion and any narration/explicit duration. For example, a one-second animation with Cut(advance_after=0.1) ends at one second even when hold=3; it does not add a three-second tail.

GIF ignores Deck narration and slide(duration=...); it uses motion, transitions, advance_after and hold. Deck.sample() uses the narration-aware video schedule, so a narrated Deck's GIF need not match its sampled duration.

The encoder shows the settled state even with hold=0, replacing the final motion shot when needed rather than always appending a full hold. A static or sub-frame slide still needs a representable frame. GIF and video durations can therefore differ slightly from the mathematical timeline. Deck video currently requires a positive hold for slides with neither narration nor an explicit positive duration; a zero hold remains valid for Canvas and Deck GIF.

docs.title: Audio, captions and reduced motion
docs.text:
MP4/WebM/MOV mix supported clip audio, Deck narration and an optional soundtrack. Narration starts at its slide's absolute offset. The soundtrack is trimmed to the visual timeline and can loop; audio padding from the codec does not extend the reported visual duration. GIF and image sequences carry no audio. Use video when the soundtrack or narration must accompany the motion. MP4 exports play layer animations and transitions while retaining per-slide narration. For still-slide narration, author static canvases and set deck.transition(Cut()).

A video layer's start is slide-local. Its trim_start, trim_end and speed select source media time; caption start/end are relative to the placed clip, not to the original source file. Captions are active over [start, end) and are burned into the foreground of supported raster/video output. They remain timed when reduced motion freezes the clip's picture.

ExportPolicy(reduced_motion=True) suppresses authored layer motion and authored slide transitions. It retains holds, narration and caption timing; default Deck crossfades can remain between slides. Use the actual export receipt for the resulting duration, rather than the original motion duration.

HTML keeps on_click cues interactive and after_previous cues automatic. advance_after enables conditional auto-advance after the incoming transition; it does not turn the presentation into fixed-duration video. Video layers use a static fallback in HTML, so their playback/caption timing is not reproduced. Check validate_export() and the returned fallback diagnostics for the target. GIF/video option families, unsupported transparency and codec rate limits fail with actionable errors rather than silently selecting another format.

docs.title: Verify playback
docs.text:
The three-slide integration scene in tests/test_video_layers.py checks actual GIF, MP4 and WebM output: selected pixels against canonical samples, incoming transitions, caption start/end windows, encoded timing, and decoded soundtrack and narration frequencies. Reduced-motion cases check frozen clip imagery and timed captions. Run it with FFmpeg and ffprobe installed:

uv run --locked pytest tests/test_video_layers.py -k motion_package --no-cov

Existing HTML timeline tests execute the JavaScript in Node stage fixtures; target-specific browser fidelity remains a separate check.

docs.text:
Import documented authoring types and result models from quickthumb, and audio analysis from the documented quickthumb.audio module. A name being importable from another module does not make it a supported entry point.

Surface Supported use Authoring Canvas, Deck, documented layer/effect models, motion tracks, transitions and option models Document operations validate(), inspect(), diagnose(), prefetch_assets(), sample() and export() on either document kind; inspect_document() for generic consumers Results Typed reports, ExportResult, CanonicalFrame / FrameSequence, and ImageSequence* results; serialize them with model_dump_json() JSON to_json(), Canvas.from_json(), Deck.from_json(), canvas_json_schema() and document_json_schema() Audio authoring quickthumb.audio.analyze_audio() and AudioAnalysis; bake source-clock onset times and RMS-driven scale into numeric motion Specialist output Documented render(), render_frame(), to_*() and export_image_sequence() methods when their return type or controls fit the task

export() is the recommended file boundary: it preflights capability policy and returns written paths and diagnostics. Specialist methods have their own return values and do not all enforce that policy; see output API. Keep format-specific options at that boundary rather than calling exporters directly.

Modules beginning with _, renderer/context objects, and timeline compilation helpers are implementation details. They can change or disappear without a supported lifecycle. Use sample() to consume frames instead of coordinating a compiler and renderer. The reference pages and generated schema describe the installed version's supported fields; public does not mean frozen across versions.

docs.title: One document workflow
docs.text:
This uses the same layer data in Python, canonical JSON and a Deck, with no renderer objects or optional dependencies:

from quickthumb import Canvas, Deck, Document, ExportResult

canvas = Canvas(320, 180).background(color="#102030").shape(
    "rectangle", position=(24, 24), width=80, height=40, color="#42CEB7",
    id="badge", motion_key="brand", anchor=(0, 0),
)
restored = Canvas.from_json(canvas.to_json())
document: Document = Deck(slides=[restored])
result: ExportResult = document.export("slides.png")
print(result.written_paths)  # Numbered paths are reported by the result.
print(document.sample().frames[0].sha256)

docs.title: Shared layer vocabulary
docs.text:
Canvas layers use the same fields when carried by a Deck slide or canonical JSON. A Deck adds slide order, transitions, narration and notes; it does not rename layer fields. Python tuples become JSON arrays, enum values become strings, and each layer has a type discriminator.

Field or concept Meaning id Optional identifier unique within a Canvas scene, including group descendants. Each Deck slide has its own identity scope. motion_key Optional matching key across scenes for Morph transitions; distinct from a scene-local id. position, width, height Authored placement and size, in pixels or percentage strings where the layer accepts them. Percentages resolve against the canvas; consult the layer reference for required fields and sizing rules. align The point of a layer's layout box placed at position; also controls text alignment. See Align. rotation, anchor Rotation is in degrees. anchor=(x, y) is a normalized 0–1 pivot for canonical motion, distinct from layout alignment. Static rotation has its own framing; see transform anchors. opacity Layer opacity from 0 to 1 where supported. animation A preset or AnimationSpec containing typed tracks and timing. Position tracks are offsets from authored placement; scale tracks transform the outer object, while ImageZoomTrack changes image content inside its frame. Group Auto-layout owns child placement. Use .group() for rows/columns rather than positioning each child. parent / null Advanced, scene-local transform hierarchy for top-level animatable layers. Child placement is parent-local; percentage coordinates still resolve against the canvas. This is separate from group layout. See parent transforms.

Not every layer accepts every field: backgrounds, outlines, nulls and drawable layers have different roles. Their reference pages and the JSON schema are the field-level contract. Plugin registrations declare parameters and can supply rendering callbacks through an explicit PluginRegistry; parsing JSON does not package or install those callbacks.
